_shape_note: This is a different content shape than the existing GS10R short-response stations (historical-context, document-use, enduring-issues) — those are type-an-answer reps; this is 4-option multiple choice, one correct answer, self-check with immediate feedback. framing: Practice, not a grade on accuracy. Answer all ten, then check your work. Full documents and short-answer practice on these same ten sources are also in the Casefile A packet in class.

items.source: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government, 1690
items.stimulus: “If man in the state of nature is free, if he is absolute lord of his own person and possessions, why will he give up his freedom? Why will he put himself under the control of any person or institution? The obvious answer is that rights in the state of nature are constantly exposed to the attack of others. Since every man is equal and since most men do not concern themselves with equity and justice, the enjoyment of rights in the state of nature is unsafe and insecure. Hence each man joins in society with others to preserve his life, liberty, and property.”
items.prompt: According to Locke, what problem do people face in the state of nature?
options: The enjoyment of their rights is unsafe and insecure
Absolute monarchs protect property better than governments do
They are not free, because they own nothing
They are prevented from joining together in society
hints: Locke says rights exist in the state of nature — he's not questioning whether people HAVE rights. Reread for what he says can go wrong with them.
Look at the words right before “insecure” in the passage — Locke names the problem directly in that sentence.

items.document: Document 2 — John Locke, on a legislature that overreaches
items.source: John Locke, Two Treatises on Civil Government
items.stimulus: “[When] the legislature shall . . . grasp [for] themselves, or put into the hands of any other, an absolute power over their lives, liberties, and estates of the people, . . . they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands for quite contrary ends, and it [passes] to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty. . . .”
items.prompt: According to this passage, what happens when a legislature seizes absolute power over the people?
options: The people must obey until the next election is held
Power passes back to the people, who may resume their original liberty
The monarch regains the authority the legislature had taken
The legislature gains the right to tax without consent
hints: Locke is describing what happens AFTER a legislature breaks its side of the deal — not what happens to the legislature itself.
The phrase “resume their original liberty” tells you who ends up holding the power.

items.document: Document 3 — Baron de Montesquieu, on the power of judging
items.source: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws
items.stimulus: “. . . Nor is there liberty if the power of judging is not separate from legislative power and from executive power. If it were joined to legislative power, the power over the life and liberty of the citizens would be arbitrary, for the judge would be the legislator. If it were joined to executive power, the judge could have the force of an oppressor. . . .”
items.prompt: This passage was written in which region, and during which movement?
options: South Asia, during the Mughal Empire
East Asia, during the Tokugawa Shogunate
Europe, during the Renaissance
Europe, during the Enlightenment
hints: This is a “where and when” question, not a “what does it say” question — three of the four options aren't even real places/movements from this unit.
Montesquieu is one of the Enlightenment philosophers you've been building a list of all week — check that list.

items.document: Document 4 — Baron de Montesquieu, on powers united
items.source: Baron de Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws
items.stimulus: “When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates [government officials], there can be no liberty; because apprehensions [fears] may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws to execute them in a tyrannical manner. . . .”
items.prompt: What problem does Montesquieu identify in this passage?
options: Concentration of power in the same hands
A shortage of natural resources
The dangers of direct democracy
Religious conflict between states
hints: The word “tyrannical” appears twice in this passage — that's the clue to the problem Montesquieu is naming.
He's describing what happens when legislative and executive power sit in the same hands — not a shortage of resources or a religious conflict.

items.source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, 1762. Translated by G. D. H. Cole, 1913. Book II, Chapter III.
items.stimulus: “There is often a great deal of difference between the will of all and the general will; the latter takes account only of the common interest, while the former takes private interest into account, and is no more than a sum of particular wills.”
items.prompt: According to Rousseau, how is the general will different from the will of all?
options: The general will is decided by a vote of the majority
The general will protects each person’s private property
The general will takes account only of the common interest
The general will belongs to the king alone
hints: Find the phrase “common interest” in the passage — that's doing the work in this question.
The “will of all” is described as private interests added up. The general will is described differently — contrast the two clauses.

items.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792. Addressed to Talleyrand-Périgord, a member of the French National Assembly.
items.stimulus: “. . . if she be not prepared by education to become the companion of man, she will stop the progress of knowledge. . . . If women are to be excluded . . . prove first . . . that they want [lack] reason, else this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION will ever show that man must . . . act like a tyrant. . . .”
items.prompt: According to this passage, what does Wollstonecraft demand of those who would exclude women?
options: That they educate women before judging them
That they first prove women lack reason
That they grant women the vote immediately
That they abolish the new constitution
hints: Look for the word “prove” in the passage — Wollstonecraft is issuing a challenge, not making a request.
She's not asking for education to happen first — she's daring her opponents to prove a claim before excluding women.

items.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792. Addressed to Talleyrand-Périgord, a member of the French National Assembly.
items.stimulus: “. . . if she be not prepared by education to become the companion of man, she will stop the progress of knowledge. . . . If women are to be excluded . . . prove first . . . that they want [lack] reason, else this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION will ever show that man must . . . act like a tyrant. . . .”
options: a French revolutionary leader addressing the National Assembly
a Russian empress addressing her nobility
a British writer addressing a member of the French National Assembly
an English philosopher addressing Parliament
hints: Talleyrand-Périgord is named in the source line as the person this letter is addressed TO — what country was he part of?
Wollstonecraft herself was British — she's writing TO a French official, not writing as one.

If women are to be excluded . . . prove first . . . that they want [lack] reason, else this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION will ever show that man must . . . act like a tyrant. . . .”
items.prompt: Which enduring issue is best supported by this passage?
options: Power and Its Abuse
Wealth and Resources
Technology and Environment
A Connected World
hints: The passage is about exclusion from reason and rights based on sex — think about which umbrella issue covers unequal treatment and authority.
This isn't about wealth, technology, or global connections — it's about who holds power over whom, and how.

items.document: Document 9 — Catherine the Great of Russia
items.source: Documents of Catherine the Great, W. F. Reddaway, ed., Cambridge University Press (adapted)
items.stimulus: “. . . The Laws ought to be so framed, as to secure the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible. . . . The Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws. . . .”
items.prompt: According to Catherine the Great, what does equality among citizens consist of?
options: Equal ownership of land
All citizens being subject to the same laws
Equal representation in an elected assembly
Freedom from taxation
hints: The second sentence of the passage defines equality directly — find the word “Equality” in the text.
She's not talking about land or representation — reread the clause right after “consists in this.”

items.document: Document 9 — Catherine the Great of Russia
items.source: Documents of Catherine the Great, W. F. Reddaway, ed., Cambridge University Press (adapted)
items.stimulus: “. . . The Laws ought to be so framed, as to secure the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible. . . . The Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws. . . .”
items.prompt: Catherine the Great ruled which state, and during which movement?
options: France, during the French Revolution
Prussia, during the Reformation
Austria, during the Industrial Revolution
Russia, during the Enlightenment
hints: Catherine the Great is one of the “enlightened” monarchs — you've grouped her with rulers who read the Enlightenment philosophers.
Her country's name gives you half the answer; the movement takes more thought — check your enlightened despots list for the other half.
